Execution coverage and parser limitations

Device model & effective policy

Every configuration is parsed into a configuration tree (AST) and a normalized schema; findings come only from structured checks evaluated against it and the device model (bindings, interface state, rule order, object groups, negation/deactivation). Results inside unapplied ACLs, disabled or deactivated policies, shut-down interfaces or negated statements are not effective. Regex/text matches are shown as informational patterns (non-finding) and are never findings. Neither counts toward metrics or compliance reports (switch the verdict filter to see them).

Vulnerability overlay (offline NVD · CISA KEV)

The firmware release parsed from each configuration is matched against a local advisory database, with feature exposure (e.g. SSL-VPN, GlobalProtect, WebVPN, HTTP server) taken from the device model. Nothing is looked up online. Bundled advisory data includes the NVD CVE API 2.0 modified feed filtered to supported product families through 2026-10-16 and CISA KEV catalog 2026.10.15. For future offline refreshes, import an NVD CVE API 2.0 JSON export, the CISA KEV catalog JSON or an NetAST advisory file via approved media.

Compliance reports

One-click, self-contained report per framework, built from effective findings and the CVE overlay. Each control is marked Finding, No automated findings — verify manually or Not assessed. This is configuration evidence, not an attestation.

Transparent by default

Rule catalog

Extensible audit catalog across 14 vendor families. Built-in vendor rules are included automatically; add custom rules whenever needed. The built-in enterprise catalog includes 180 vendor-specific controls across the 14 supported families. No rule-count or size limit: custom rules are saved in this browser's IndexedDB, bounded only by available disk space. Very large catalogs mainly increase scan time. Coverage is not an official compliance benchmark.

Seed IDs, patterns, severity and remediation strings are retained exactly as supplied. Additional context checks avoid cross-policy matches and mark questionable assumptions as review-only. These are not official CIS benchmark mappings.

Browser-owned state

Local settings

Your configurations and audit evidence live in memory, not local storage.

Persistence & privacy

Custom rule definitions and disabled rule IDs are stored in IndexedDB with no rule-count or rule-pack size limit (only the disk space the browser grants applies); UI preferences use localStorage. If IndexedDB is unavailable, NetAST falls back to localStorage (~5 MB). If a write ever fails, NetAST warns you and keeps the newest changes for this session only, so export rule packs for durable backup. Custom rules can contain sensitive strings: do not put production secrets in them. Storage may be unavailable in a sandbox or private browsing.

Encrypted local-state backup

Export custom rules, disabled-rule IDs, triage, preferences and local overrides as an AES-256-GCM encrypted backup. A fresh 256-bit password is generated for every export. Save it in your approved enterprise password manager before confirming. Only the exported backup file is encrypted; active browser storage remains browser-managed plaintext.

Encrypted backup recommended after every custom-rule or golden-baseline change.

Key derivation uses PBKDF2-SHA-256 (310,000 iterations) with a random salt and AES-256-GCM. The tool never stores the password; there is no recovery mechanism.

Air-gapped operation

This build contains no remote resources, telemetry or update checks. The page Content-Security-Policy forbids every network API (fetch, XHR, WebSocket, beacons, remote images, form posts), so not even injected code can phone home. Advisory updates are file imports.

Run once after loading on the target terminal. Screenshot the displayed failure/block message as auditable evidence that CSP isolation is working; retain the screenshot with deployment records.

File buffers are zeroed right after decoding. JavaScript cannot wipe the browser heap directly; dropping every reference and reloading the tab (emergency purge, idle purge) makes the engine discard it.

Baseline audit layer · implicit defaults

Profile shifts baseline severities only; per-check overrides take precedence.

Structured checks that raise a finding when a mandatory control is missing or a permissive platform default is in force: an implicit outbound deny block that is completely absent, blank or replaced by a permit default, global logging that is completely absent or blank/disabled, no default-deny (implicit permit-all), no centralized AAA, no NTP, no banner, no idle timeout. Every finding states whether the block is absent or present but blank. Absence is evaluated on the parsed configuration tree and device model, including platform defaults — never by text search. Severities are graded (Critical: implicit outbound deny missing, global logging missing, default-deny missing · High: AAA · Medium: NTP, banner, idle timeout) and can be overridden per check; overrides are kept in this browser and apply to counts, metrics, reports and compliance exports.

Scope & safe operation

Parser support and limitations are summarized in the Workspace parser support matrix. NetAST is an independent pattern-audit tool, not a complete vendor parser, certification, exploitability assessment or substitute for release-specific validation.

NetAST is an independent pattern-audit implementation, not affiliated with any vendor or commercial audit product. It is not equivalent to a commercial parser, an exploitability assessment or a complete CIS audit.

Matched source evidence

Remediation recommendation · manual only
Recommendations are guidance, not executable scripts or proof that a setting is wrong. Bracketed values are placeholders. Confirm device model, software release, effective configuration, business dependencies and official vendor guidance before any change. NetAST never applies or executes remediation.
Pattern and evaluation


Add custom rule
Use named regex groups (Python style (?P<name>...) or JavaScript style (?<name>...)). Captured names populate matching remediation tokens such as {{ custom_zone }} from matched evidence.
Enter regex backslashes normally here. JSON exports escape them automatically. Multi-line regex is evaluated per structural block (64 KiB window) as an informational pattern (non-finding) only; on files larger than 5 MiB (streamed in chunks), multi-line regex rules are skipped and a prominent Audit Findings warning reports the count; single-line contains/regex indicators still run in the analysis workers. Findings always come from the structured engines, which run on every chunk. Block absence rules flag a finding when the pattern is MISSING: with a structural context, the pattern must appear inside every matching block (for example, "transport input ssh" inside each "line vty" block); empty context requires the pattern anywhere in the document. Remediation text supports auto-resolved tokens — {{ rule_id }}, {{ target_interface }}, {{ target_vty }}, {{ target_acl }}, {{ target_policy_id }}, {{ target_object }}, {{ target_device }} — populated per finding in CLI and Ansible exports. Suspicious regex is rejected, the regex clock halts slow rules, and the secrets linter blocks plaintext credentials before anything persists. Import rule packs only from trusted sources.
